## Code is the source of your screens

A screen's source of truth is its code: the file in `src/screens/`, built from the Sando units and
tokens your repository installed. `design/SCREENS.md` states what the screen is meant to hold; the
code is what the screen is. When the two disagree, fix whichever is wrong, in the same change.

Your service's Figma file, if it keeps one, is downstream of the code. It is assembled from Sando
library instances to mirror what the code renders ([`figma-library.md`](figma-library.md)), and a
change made only in Figma is not a change to the screen until the code carries it.

This is the same stance Sando takes for itself. Sando's code is the source of its units and tokens,
and the Sando Figma library is a projection of that code. Your repository applies the rule one level
up: Sando's code is the source of the units, your code is the source of the screens, and each Figma
file mirrors the code it belongs to.

## Building a screen: the reading order

When an agent is asked to build or change a screen, it reads in this order. Each step narrows the
one before it and never overrides it.

1. **The Sando guide**, `docs/sando/`. The `AGENTS.md` snippet in
   [`getting-started.md`](getting-started.md) § For your coding agent points the agent there: how to
   compose, space, size and style. These are the floors every product keeps.
2. **`design/DESIGN.md`**: what the service is, who uses it, its UX policy and design language.
3. **The screen's entry in `design/SCREENS.md`**: its purpose, section stack, states and copy, and the
   flows in `SCREENS.md` § Flows that pass through it. If the screen has no entry, write the entry first and have it confirmed; a screen never invents its
   anatomy or its copy.
4. **`design/product.json`**: the `compose` and `usage` rules and the `policy` for each unit the
   screen places, the `contexts` it runs in and its `lang`. A screen imports only units in `units` or
   `src/local/`; to use another Sando unit, add it to `units` and run `npm run sando:install`.
5. **[`missing-units.md`](missing-units.md)**, when no installed unit renders a part of the entry.

Then build it:

6. **Keep the screen pure** (§ Screens and service logic): it takes its data, the current time and
   its URL state as props, and leaves fetching, storage and navigation to the route layer.
7. **Write its stories**: a `Default` story, and one story per state its `SCREENS.md` entry lists
   under N.3, named as N.3 names it.
8. **Check it**: `npm run sando:check` runs the static checks, then renders the screen in every story,
   width, colour scheme and theme. Open the screenshots it writes under
   `.sando/verify/screens/<Name>/` and look at them; a passing report does not show you a wrong
   layout. Fix what either shows, then run `npm run sando:review -- <Name>` for a design review,
   which reports and never blocks.

## Screens and service logic

A screen renders from its props alone. Then every state of every screen can be rendered, checked and
reviewed without a backend, a router or a signed-in user, and the same screen serves your app, its
stories and a design review.

### Where the logic lives

The code that fetches data, reads and writes the URL, stores state and navigates lives in a **route
layer** that renders the screen with props. Where that layer sits is your framework's choice, and no
check reads its path:

| Your repository | The route layer | The entry |
|---|---|---|
| Vite with no router, or a library router (the default) | `src/app/routes/<Name>.tsx`, with the route table in `src/app/routes.tsx` | `src/app/main.tsx` (several pages: `src/app/<page>-page.tsx`) |
| React Router v7, framework mode | `app/routes/*.tsx`: a `loader` and `action`, and a component that renders `<Name {...loaderData} />` | `app/root.tsx` |
| Next.js App Router | `src/app/**/page.tsx` fetches the data and renders `<Name />` across the client boundary | the framework |
| TanStack Router, file routes | the `loader` in `src/routes/*.tsx` | `src/main.tsx` |

URL state (a step, a tab, a filter) reaches the screen as a prop such as `step`, and the screen
reports a change through a callback such as `onStepChange`, which the route layer writes back to the
URL.

### What a screen may not do

These break rendering a state from props, so the ESLint rules refuse them in `src/screens/**`:

| Kind | Refused |
|---|---|
| Network | `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest`, `WebSocket`, `EventSource`, `navigator.sendBeacon` |
| Storage | `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, `indexedDB`, `caches`, `document.cookie` |
| URL and navigation | `location`, `history`, `window.open`, `window.parent`, `top`, `opener`, `postMessage` |
| Time | `Date.now()`, `Date()` and `new Date()` with no argument, `performance.now()`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `requestAnimationFrame` |
| Randomness | `Math.random()`, `crypto.randomUUID()`, `crypto.getRandomValues()` |
| Global DOM | `document`, any `window.*`, `globalThis.*` or `self.*`, a global `addEventListener`, `scrollTo`, `matchMedia` |
| Effects | `useEffect`, `useLayoutEffect`, `useInsertionEffect`, `useSyncExternalStore` |
| Imports | another screen, a Sando unit not in `units`, `react-dom/client`, a global sheet under `src/styles/`, `import.meta.env`, and any module your `policy.screen.denyImports` names |

Everything else is allowed: React's state hooks, `use` and `useContext` (for i18n, theme and form
contexts), i18n and form libraries, an analytics call inside an event handler, and static imports
of files under `src/assets/`.

- **Time is a prop.** A screen that shows a countdown or "today" takes `now` (an ISO string) from its
  route and its stories.
- **A shared page frame** (header, navigation, footer) is rendered by each screen from
  `src/screens/lib/`, and the data it needs arrives in the screen's props, never through a hidden
  context, so a story can fill it.
- **A screen shown over another** (a form over a list) takes the screen beneath as a `background`
  slot, so each renders on its own.
- **One exception**: a viewport hook in `src/screens/lib/` may read `matchMedia` through
  `useSyncExternalStore`. Try the `Show` layout first; it does the same in CSS.
- **Widen or narrow the list** in `design/product.json` `policy.screen`: `denyImports` adds modules a
  screen may not import (your API client, your store), and `allowGlobals` admits a refused name, each
  with a `because`.
- `src/local/` is not held to this list: a unit may own its behaviour.

### Stories: the props of each state

Each screen has a `src/screens/<Name>.stories.tsx` in Component Story Format 3, the format Storybook
and Ladle read, which `sando verify` reads without either:

```tsx
// src/screens/PlanList.stories.tsx
import { PlanList } from "./PlanList";
import plans from "../app/data/plans.snapshot.json"; // a committed snapshot is fine
export default { component: PlanList };
export const Default = { args: { now: "2026-11-07T09:00:00+09:00", plans, favorites: ["p3"] } };
export const Empty = { args: { ...Default.args, plans: [] } };
```

- `Default` is required. Every other export is a state its `SCREENS.md` entry names under N.3.
- A story holds data, never logic: it may import any data, and makes no request. To show real data,
  import a committed JSON snapshot; the script that refreshes it is yours.
- Time is a fixed string, and a content image is a file under `src/assets/`.

## design/product.json

The part of the design language a script can read. The Sando CLI reads it (`sando install` installs
what it lists, the checks hold your code to it), and so do your agents. Its JSON Schema ships in
the CLI, at `node_modules/@sando-ui/cli/schema/product.schema.json`, and `sando check` validates
the file against it.

```json
{
  "name": "<field>",
  "title": "<Product title>",
  "description": "<What the service is, in one or two sentences>",
  "prefix": "<xy->",
  "theme": "<brand>",
  "lang": "<language tag>",
  "units": ["app-shell", "navbar", "stack", "text", "<item>"],
  "compose": [
    {
      "unit": "app-shell",
      "props": { "bottomNav": "bottom-nav-docked" },
      "rule": "<When and why the unit is composed this way>"
    }
  ],
  "usage": [],
  "contexts": [],
  "policy": {}
}
```

| Field | Type | Means |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | A slug naming the product by its field, never by a company. |
| `title` | string | The product's display name. |
| `description` | string | What the service is. `DESIGN.md` § 0 says the rest. |
| `prefix` | string | The class prefix of your own CSS (`tc-`), never `sd-` ([`styling-contract.md`](styling-contract.md)). Optional; the CSS rules check your class names against it once it is set. |
| `theme` | string or string[] | The brand the product uses, by slug. `sando install` installs `brand-<theme>`, and the same slug goes on `<html data-brand>` ([`getting-started.md`](getting-started.md) § Choose the brand on `<html>`, [`theming.md`](theming.md) § One theme per product). A product that truly ships under several brands lists them, and `sando verify` renders every screen in each. |
| `lang` | string | The language of the product's copy, as a BCP 47 tag (`en`, `ko`). It goes on `<html lang>`. |
| `units` | string[] | The Sando item names (`plan-card`, `stack`) of every Layout, Component and Block that a file under `src/screens/` (the screens and `lib/`) imports directly, each once. A unit a screen imports is listed **even when another listed unit already brings it**: `sando check` blocks the import otherwise. A unit no screen imports, which arrives only because a listed unit or a `src/local/` unit depends on it, is not listed: the install brings it, and listing it would be a second copy of the dependency graph. The brand, `styles` and `guide` are never listed; the first comes from `theme` and the other two with every install. How to derive the list is below. |
| `compose` | object[] | How units fit together on this product's screens. Each entry is `unit` (one of `units`), `props` (a slot prop of that unit mapped to the item that fills it, each value also one of `units`; `{}` when the rule names no slot) and `rule` (the sentence that says when and why). |
| `usage` | object[] | Which size or variant a unit takes in a position on this product's screens, narrowing [`prop-usage-contract.md`](prop-usage-contract.md) and never overriding it. Each entry is `unit` and `rule`. |
| `contexts` | string[] | The `data-context` values the product runs in ([`theming.md`](theming.md) § Usage context). Empty means the brand's own sizes. |
| `policy` | object | The part of your UX policy a check can hold the code to (below). Optional; a key left out enforces nothing. |
| `sando` | object | `{ "version", "registry", "installedAt" }`: the Sando version installed and the registry it came from. Written by `sando install`, never by hand. |

Every field from `name` to `contexts` is present in every file. A list the product has nothing for
is `[]`, never left out, so an agent can tell "no rule" from "not written yet".

### Deriving `units`

Two checks read imports of `src/components/`, `src/blocks/` and `src/layouts/`, at two scopes:

- In every file under `src/screens/` (screens and `lib/`, not stories), the imported unit must be in
  `units` (`sando/screen-imports`, S7).
- In every file of yours under `src/` (`src/local/` and `src/app/` included), the imported file must
  be installed, which is recorded in `design/sando.lock.json` (`sando/installed-units`, U1). A
  `src/local/` unit may import anything the install brought, listed or not.

So `units` is the set of units your screens import, no more and no less. To derive it, list the
imports in `src/screens/` that land in one of the three unit directories, and turn each file name
into its item name: the PascalCase name in kebab case (`PlanCard.tsx` is `plan-card`, `AppShell.tsx`
is `app-shell`). When you add an import to a screen, add the unit to `units` in the same change and
run `npm run sando:install`. When you remove the last screen import of a unit, take it out of
`units`; its files stay while another unit still depends on them.

### policy

Write a rule of your service here when a check can decide it; keep it in `DESIGN.md` Part 2 when it
takes judgment. The Sando checks read it, so you never write a lint rule of your own:

```json
"policy": {
  "screens": { "Home": { "type": "hub" }, "PlanApplyForm": { "type": "flow" } },
  "screenTypes": {
    "hub": { "allowUnits": ["*"], "denyUnits": ["app-bar"] },
    "flow": { "denyUnits": ["bottom-nav-docked", "footer"] }
  },
  "props": [
    { "unit": "button", "inside": "floating-toolbar", "prop": "size", "allow": ["small"], "because": "DESIGN.md § 4" }
  ],
  "budgets": { "primaryPerViewport": 1, "primaryPerScreen": 2 },
  "screen": { "denyImports": ["src/app/api/*"], "allowGlobals": [] },
  "render": { "timezone": "Asia/Seoul" }
}
```

| Key | Means |
|---|---|
| `screens` | Each screen's type, by its name in `src/screens/`. A screen left out has no type limits. |
| `screenTypes` | Which units a screen of that type may place. A unit is its item name, as in `units`; `allowUnits` absent or `"*"` means every installed unit, and `denyUnits` wins. The check reads the JSX of the screen's own file and of every `src/screens/lib/` module it imports, so a unit a shared frame places counts for each screen that renders the frame, even one the frame places only on some props: split a frame that differs by screen type. A type's `budgets` overrides `policy.budgets` key by key for its screens (`"scan": { "budgets": { "primaryPerViewport": 0 } }`). |
| `props` | Which values a unit's prop may take, optionally only `inside` another unit in the same file, with the `because` that sends a reader to the rule. |
| `budgets` | How many primary buttons are visible in one viewport (default 1), and in a whole screen (unchecked unless set). Only the topmost layer counts: buttons behind an open modal dialog, or under `inert` or `aria-hidden`, do not. A screen type's `budgets` overrides these. |
| `screen` | `denyImports`: globs a screen may not import. `allowGlobals`: names refused in § Screens and service logic that your screens may use, each as `{ "name", "because" }`. |
| `render` | The `timezone` the renders run in (default UTC), the colour `schemes` they render (default `["light", "dark"]`; `["light"]` for a product with no dark mode), and the HTML `pages` whose `<html>` R3 reads (default `["index.html"]`; list the pages your build writes, as `["dist/index.html"]`, when your repository has no root `index.html`, and build them before `sando verify`, since a listed page that does not exist is an R3 finding). |

## sando install: the installed set follows product.json

`sando install` (the `sando:install` script) installs the brand of every `theme` and every unit in
`units`, at the Sando version `sando.version` records, so the installed set always matches
`design/product.json`. Run it after adding a unit to `units`. How it installs, what it records and
how it moves you to another version are [`getting-started.md`](getting-started.md) § Install units
and § Upgrading.

Removing a unit from `units` does not delete its files: delete them by hand, after checking that no
other unit still imports them, then run `sando install` so the lock forgets them.

## The principles of DESIGN.md

**Sando units at their own sizes; roles and tokens, never values.** That one sentence opens every
`DESIGN.md`, and everything below applies it.

- **Name roles, not values.** Values live in the theme: colours, the type ladder, space, radius,
  control heights, motion, the page grid. `DESIGN.md` says which role a value plays and where it is
  spent: "money is `text.brand`", "secondary text is `Text tone="muted"`", "cards take the large
  radius". It never writes a hex, a pixel size or a font size. A value written into the design
  language is a second copy of the theme, and the first theme change makes it false.
- **A reference measurement picks a role or a rung; it never resizes a unit.** If the product is
  modelled on a reference (a live service, a mockup, a competitor), measure it, and use each
  measurement as evidence for which role, size or rung to choose: `size="small"`, a `title` role, a
  section gap. Never inline a size, padding, gap or font value to match the reference, and never
  squeeze a unit into the reference's pixels. Where a unit at its own sizes cannot carry the look,
  that is a gap to raise ([`missing-units.md`](missing-units.md)), not a value to force.
- **Where the theme departs from the reference on purpose, follow the theme.** A contrast floor or a
  ladder decision outranks the reference. Record the departure once, in the open-with-the-theme
  section, so nobody "fixes" it back.
- **Compose, do not restyle.** Every pattern is rendered by a named Sando unit with named props, or is
  listed as a gap. The rules for composing are [`composition-contract.md`](composition-contract.md)
  and [`spacing-contract.md`](spacing-contract.md); `DESIGN.md` narrows them for the product and never
  overrides them.
- **Measured, not imagined.** Say where the language came from (what was measured, at which widths,
  on which dates), so a later reader can tell a decision from a guess.
- **Name no real company.** A reference service is written as a placeholder (`{svc}`), in quoted copy
  too, and sample company data is invented. Your design files describe your product, not someone
  else's.
- **Gaps go upstream.** A pattern the design system cannot render yet is listed in the units section
  as a gap and requested from Sando. The product does not fork a unit to close it.

## Template for DESIGN.md

Copy these headings into `DESIGN.md`. Each section answers one question; leave a section out only if
the product truly has nothing to say there, and say so in one line rather than deleting it silently.

The file opens with a title and the opening, then has **two parts, kept apart** under their own `##`
headings, so a reader can tell what every Sando product shares from what this service decided. The
numbered sections are `###` headings inside Part 2. This is the whole outline, at its heading
levels:

```markdown
# <Product>: design language

<the opening: § Opening below>

## Part 1: Shared UX principles

<pointers into the Sando guide: § Part 1 below>

## Part 2: This service's UX policy

### 0. The product and its context
### 1. The language
### 2. Foundations, as roles
### 2.5 Open with the theme
### 3. Layout and columns
### 4. Chrome
### 5. How screens are used
### 6. Composition
### 7. Elements: when to use, when not
### 8. Which unit renders each pattern
### 9. Voice and tone
### 10. Not observed, do not copy
### 11. Accessibility commitments
```

Keep the two `##` headings exactly as written. `sando check` (S6) looks for `## Part 1` and
`## Part 2`, and `sando review` takes everything from the first `##` heading after
`## Part 1: Shared UX principles` as the service's policy, so Part 1 has no `##` heading inside it.
A reference to "`DESIGN.md` § 2" means section 2 of Part 2.

### Opening

One paragraph on what the file is for, the source of the measurements, and a table of the layers:
the design system decides what a unit is; the theme decides every value; this file decides where,
how much and why those values are spent; a sibling `SCREENS.md` holds per-screen specs (each
screen's section stack, its states and its verbatim strings), so a builder never invents copy or
anatomy. Then the principle sentence above, verbatim.

### Part 1: Shared UX principles

A short section that **points at the Sando guide and restates none of it**: which unit does a job,
when not to use it and what it pairs with ([`component-usage.md`](component-usage.md),
[`block-index.md`](block-index.md)); how units compose and the accessibility a screen owes
([`composition-contract.md`](composition-contract.md)); spacing
([`spacing-contract.md`](spacing-contract.md)); size and variant by position
([`prop-usage-contract.md`](prop-usage-contract.md)); what to do when no unit fits
([`missing-units.md`](missing-units.md)). A copy goes stale at the next Sando release, and a reader
cannot tell a copy from a decision. Where the service narrows one of these rules, say so in Part 2 and
link the rule it narrows.

### Part 2: This service's UX policy

Sections 0 to 11 below. Between them they must answer, for this service only: the flows between
screens (§ 0 journeys, drawn screen by screen in `SCREENS.md` § Flows), its domain rules (§ 0), how
loading, empty and error states read (§ 5), its copy tone (§ 9) and its accessibility commitments
(§ 11).

A rule a check can decide (which units a screen type may place, which size a unit takes in a
position, how many primaries a viewport holds) goes in `design/product.json` `policy`, and Part 2
names it there rather than restating it. Part 2 keeps what takes judgment: density, hierarchy, tone.

### 0. The product and its context

- **What it is**: the service in a paragraph, its businesses or areas, and a sitemap.
- **The journeys** every screen serves, numbered, each ending where the user commits.
- **Domain rules**: what the business requires of every screen (who is eligible, what must stand next
  to a price, which notices are legal obligations), each as a sentence a screen can be checked against.
- **Context**: who uses it, on which device, in what state of mind, and what a screen must do for
  them. Which usage context (`data-context`) the product runs in, if not the default.

### 1. The language

- **Brand language**: three to five traits, each with the on-screen behaviour that carries it and a
  line of evidence.
- **Expression strength**: how much brand colour, decoration and motion a screen spends.
- **What the product never does.**
- **The language in ten rules**: short, numbered, each one checkable on a screen.

### 2. Foundations, as roles

- **Colour roles**: a table of the product's role (brand action, ink, muted, decorative line, ...),
  the Sys role it maps to, and where it is spent.
- **Type roles**: a table of each text job (page heading, card headline, body, caption, badge) and
  the `Text` variant, size and emphasis that carry it, per breakpoint step. Then the pairings
  (heading and sub, number and unit, label and value), which matter more than sizes.
- **Shape, elevation, motion**: which radius tier, shadow role and motion role each kind of surface
  takes.
- **Scale feel**: density, how close the type ladder is, which control heights do the work, what
  changes at each breakpoint step.

### 2.5 Open with the theme

A table of what the reference uses that the theme does not carry, and whose call each is (the
theme's, the design system's, the product owner's). Then what is settled and must not be reopened.

### 3. Layout and columns

How each page type is arranged on a phone and from the large step up, with the grid span and the
Layout unit that does it. Then the layout rules (what never goes multi-column, where the action moves
on a wide screen).

### 4. Chrome

The header, bottom navigation, sticky action bars, footer and overlays, phone against wide screen.

### 5. How screens are used

The screen jobs (scan, decide, commit, or the product's own), the container ladder (tooltip, popover,
sheet, dialog, page) with when to use each, disclosure depths, how context is asked for and
remembered, how comparison works, how loading, empty and error states read (what each says and
offers next), and how every terminal state avoids a dead end.

### 6. Composition

- **The section template** and its variants.
- **Section order** on each page type, with which slots are fixed.
- **Grouping**: band, card, well, hairline, and when each is used.
- **Budgets per viewport**: how many filled primaries, brand figures, badges and alarm colours.
- **Alignment** and **density**, then **page archetypes**.
- **Review checklist**: a table of checks a screen must pass, each with the product's own value. Add
  a row whenever a review finds a defect in a draft, so the same defect is caught next time. This is
  the product's list; the design system's own review criteria still apply underneath it.

### 7. Elements: when to use, when not

Colour, type in use, badges and chips, icons and imagery, shadow and border, interaction states: each
with its job and its "never". If the product makes its own imagery, its brief and canvas sizes go
here.

### 8. Which unit renders each pattern

A table of every recurring pattern, the Sando unit and props that render it, and a note. Name the
size or variant to pick, never a value to set. The last row lists the patterns with **no unit yet**;
each is a gap requested upstream ([`missing-units.md`](missing-units.md)), with the local bridge that
stands in for it if there is one.

### 9. Voice and tone

Register (and how it shifts with the screen's job), headings, copy by situation, buttons and links,
money, numbers and punctuation, emoji.

### 10. Not observed, do not copy

What the measurements could not see (so nobody invents it), what the reference does that the product
must not copy (inaccessible patterns among them), and where any reference marks are kept locally and
never shipped.

### 11. Accessibility commitments

What this service promises beyond the guide's floors, never fewer: a reading level, a minimum type
role for its audience, a usage context (`data-context`) it supports, how it serves assistive
technology on its own flows. The floors themselves are the guide's
([`composition-contract.md`](composition-contract.md)); this section only adds.

## Template for SCREENS.md

`DESIGN.md` says how every screen behaves; `SCREENS.md` says what one screen holds, closely enough that
an agent can build it without inventing anything. Copy this shape. Numbers in an entry are evidence
for which role, size or rung to pick, never values to set: the principles above apply here too.

The checks read this file by its headings, so the outline is exact:

```markdown
# <Product>: screen specs

<where the specs came from, and the screens it covers>

## Conventions

## Flows

## 1. Home

### 1.1 Purpose, entry, exits
### 1.2 Section table
### 1.3 States
### 1.4 Strings
### 1.5 Notes

## 2. PlanList

### 2.1 Purpose, entry, exits
...
```

- **A screen entry is a `##` heading of a number from 1, a dot, a space and the screen's name**,
  exactly the name of its file `src/screens/<Name>.tsx` (`## 2. PlanList` for `PlanList.tsx`), and
  nothing after it but one optional note in parentheses (`## 4. PlanFinder (questionnaire)`).
  `sando check` (S2) matches entries to screen files by that name, and `sando verify` and
  `sando review` find an entry the same way.
- **No other `##` heading starts with a number.** `## Conventions` and `## Flows` are unnumbered, so
  they are never read as a screen. A heading that breaks the entry grammar is not an entry either:
  `## 0. Conventions`, `## 3. Plan list` (more words than a name) or a lettered appendix
  (`## A. Glossary`) is skipped, so a screen whose heading drifts reads as having no entry.
- **Inside an entry, the five parts are `###` headings numbered after it** (`### 2.3 States`), in this
  order. `sando check` (S4) reads the state names under N.3, and `sando verify` (R7) the strings
  under N.4.

### Header

A title (`# <Product>: screen specs`) and one paragraph on where the specs came from: a brief, a
design, or measurements of a reference, with the widths and dates. If a reference service is
measured, name it with a placeholder (`{svc}`) everywhere, quoted copy included. Then the list of
screens the file covers, each name matching its file in `src/screens/`.

### Conventions

What every entry assumes, said once, under `## Conventions`:

- **Widths**: a table of the breakpoint steps the entries use and what changes at each (type step
  only, columns, chrome swap).
- **Roles**: type and colour are written as the roles `DESIGN.md` § 2 names, so an entry never needs
  a value.
- **Chrome summary**: the header, bottom navigation and footer each page type carries, so an entry
  repeats chrome only where it differs.

### Flows

Every journey from `DESIGN.md` § 0, drawn through this product's screens under `## Flows`: the
screens in order, the action that moves the user from each to the next, and where the flow ends. Each
screen in `src/screens/` sits on at least one flow, and each screen's exits (N.1) agree with the
flows. This section is the one place flows live; keep no separate flow file.

```markdown
1. **<Journey>.** Home (`<action>`) > ItemList (`<action>`) > ItemDetail (`<action>`) >
   ApplyForm, ending in <the commit>.
```

### N. ScreenName

One `## N. <Name>` section per screen, numbered from 1 in the order you like, headed with the name of
its file in `src/screens/`.

`### N.1 Purpose, entry, exits`

- **Purpose**: one sentence, naming the screen's job (`DESIGN.md` § 5).
- **Entry**: every way a user arrives.
- **Exits**: every action and where it leads, so no state is a dead end.

`### N.2 Section table`: the anatomy, top to bottom.

| # | Section | Contents | Phone | Each wider step it changes at | Sticky / fixed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Header | what it shows | role, size, layout | what moves | sticky or none |
| 1 | <Section> | the parts, in order | ... | ... | ... |

Then one line on rhythm (section and heading gaps as `spacing-contract.md` positions) and how the
columns split from the wide step up.

`### N.3 States`: each of these, or "not applicable" or "not observed" in its place, never silently
left out:

- first visit, loading, empty, error;
- live content (timers, autoplay), hover and focus;
- signed in against signed out;
- disabled, selected, ended or sold out.

Name each state that applies after the story that renders it, in backticks (`Empty`, `LoadError`):
the screen's stories file exports one story per name, and `sando check` matches the two. It reads
every backticked name that starts with a capital letter in N.3 as a state, so backtick nothing else
of that shape there.

`### N.4 Strings`: every visible string, verbatim, in the product's `lang`, grouped by section, each in
backticks. `sando verify` (R7) looks for every backticked string here in the renders; several
short strings may share one pair of backticks, split by ` · `, and each is looked for; a string with
a `{placeholder}` is not. The screen's `h1` is one of these strings
([`composition-contract.md`](composition-contract.md) § Accessibility you owe). Sample data is marked as sample; a company's
identity (legal name, registration numbers, address) is always placeholder data, never a real
company's.

`### N.5 Notes` (optional): open questions and known differences between the built screen and this
entry, each dated.

## A finding becomes a rule

When a review of a built screen finds a defect, fix the screen, then classify the defect so it cannot
come back. One question decides it: **would the same defect appear in another product that uses the
same units and follows the same guide?**

| The defect comes from | It is | Record it |
|---|---|---|
| A unit that renders or behaves wrong, a guide rule that is wrong or silent, a pairing or a choice of unit the guide never states | **shared** | An issue on the Sando repository (below). Sando answers with a guide rule or a unit change, which reaches every product when it reinstalls. |
| A choice this service made: its flows, its domain rules, its tone, its density, a screen's content | **service-specific** | `design/DESIGN.md` (the section it belongs to, and a row in the § 6 review checklist) or the screen's `design/SCREENS.md` entry. |

When unsure, treat it as shared, as [`missing-units.md`](missing-units.md) does for units: a shared
defect kept local is caught again by every other product.

**The intake for a shared finding** is an issue on the Sando repository titled
`[finding] <unit or guide file>: <the defect in one line>`, carrying:

- **a screenshot** of the defect, with the width and the theme it was taken at;
- **the spec** the screen was built from: its `SCREENS.md` entry, or the part of it that matters;
- **the rule it broke**, as the guide file and section, or "no rule covers this" with the rule you
  would expect;
- **the composition**: the units and props the screen used at that point;
- **the Sando version**: the contents of `docs/sando/VERSION`.

The repository's **Finding** issue form asks for exactly these, plus the unit or guide file and the
defect from the title. `sando review` writes this body for you: for each failure it judges shared,
it writes `.sando/review/<Name>/issues/<id>.md` with these fields filled from its evidence. Read it
against the screenshot before you file it; the review can be wrong.

A missing unit is the same intake with [`missing-units.md`](missing-units.md) § Asking upstream as its
contents.

## Where your design files live

All of the above lives in your own repository, and you edit it there. Sando ships units, themes and
this guide; it never ships a product's design files, and nothing in Sando knows which products use it.
When you update Sando, its changelog says what moved: where a unit, a prop or a role your
`DESIGN.md`, `SCREENS.md` or `product.json` names has changed, update the file in the same change. A
pattern the design system cannot render yet is a gap you ask for upstream
([`missing-units.md`](missing-units.md)), never a fork of an installed unit.

# Figma library: designing a product's screens with Sando in Figma

How a product's screens are designed in Figma on top of the Sando library: where the screens live,
how to enable the library, how to put a frame in your brand without painting a mix of two brands, and
what to do when a unit is missing. It is the Figma half of the same rules your code follows.

Hand-maintained; no check reads this file. The collection names below are the Sando library's as of
2026-11-06.

## Where screens live

**A product's screens live in a Figma file of the product's own**, which subscribes to the Sando
library. The Sando file holds the design system only: its components, variables and text styles. Do
not design product screens in the Sando file, and do not copy Sando components into your product
file.

It is the same split as the code. Sando's repository holds the units; your service's repository
installs them. In Figma, the library is the install: when Sando publishes a change, your file is
offered the update and you accept it, instead of re-copying anything.

Your Figma file is downstream of your code. The screens' source is `src/screens/`, and the Figma
file is assembled from Sando library instances to mirror what that code renders, as
[`design-language.md`](design-language.md) § Code is the source of your screens states.

## Enable the library

**The Sando library has to be published before any product file can enable it.** Publishing is an
action of Sando's owner, and today it has not happened: measured 2026-11-08, the Sando file
publishes no components and no variables, so the library does not appear in your file's library
list yet. Until it does, there is nothing to subscribe to and no update to accept; ask upstream
when it will be published. The steps below apply from then on.

In your product file, open the assets panel's library list and enable the Sando library. Its
components, variables and text styles then appear beside your own. Use them from there: place
components as instances, and bind fills, strokes, spacing, radius and type to Sando's variables and
text styles, never to a typed-in value. The rule for values is the one your CSS follows:
[`styling-contract.md`](styling-contract.md).

## Set the brand on both Ref and Sys

Sando's variables sit in collections by tier and domain. The **Ref** collections hold the raw scales
(`Ref Color`, `Ref Dimension`, `Ref Typography`, `Ref Radius`, `Ref Border`, `Ref Effect`,
`Ref Layer`, `Ref Motion`); the **Sys** collections hold the roles that alias them (`Sys Color`,
`Sys Dimension`, `Sys Typography`, `Sys Radius`, and the rest named `Sys ...`). Every Ref and Sys
collection carries one mode per brand; a mode is named for the brand, plus the axis that collection
already had (`<brand>-light`, `<brand>-dark`, `<brand>-small`, `<brand>-medium`, `<brand>-large`).
The `Cmp` collection has no brand modes: it aliases Sys roles and follows them.

**On every screen frame, set your brand's mode on every Ref and every Sys collection, together.**

Setting only the Sys collections looks done and is not. A variable that aliases across collections
resolves in the mode of the frame it is used in, so a Sys role set to your brand still reads its Ref
rung in whatever mode Ref is in, which is the library's default brand. The frame then paints a hybrid
of two brands: your brand's role mapping over another brand's raw values. The difference is not
subtle; measured on 2026-08-20, 430 of the 546 Ref rungs the brands share differ from one brand to
the next.

Set the brand once, on the top frame of a screen, and let children inherit it. Pick the light or dark
mode, and the `small`, `medium` or `large` step, on the same frame in the same pass.

## Never detach

**Never detach a Sando component instance.** A detached instance is a copy: it stops receiving the
library's updates, and nothing marks it as different from the real component, so the screen and the
code drift apart without anyone seeing it. Change an instance through its properties and variants
only. If they cannot express what the screen needs, the component has a gap.

## A missing unit

A missing component or block follows the same rule in Figma as in code:
[`missing-units.md`](missing-units.md). A Component is always Sando's, and so is a Block another
product would use: ask upstream, and until it ships, build a local stand-in in your product file from
Sando instances and variables, named so it is plainly local, and replace it with the library
component once it is published. Only a composition unique to your product stays in your file for
good.

# Getting started with Sando UI

How to install Sando UI units into an app of your own, which global stylesheets to load, the tools
that install and check them, how to upgrade, and what to tell the coding agent that works in your
repo. It also maps the rest of this guide. Read it once when you set up; come back to § Upgrading
each time Sando ships.

Hand-maintained. It states no token value, so no brand can make it wrong; the file paths and CLI
flags are the ones measured on a pilot install with shadcn CLI 4.23.0.

## Before you start

- A React app with TypeScript and a bundler that imports `.css` files from modules (the pilot is
  Vite with React 19).
- Node 22.13 or later with `npm`, to run the Sando tools (§ Install the tools).
- No Tailwind. Sando styles are plain CSS on custom properties, and nothing here needs it.

## Write `components.json` by hand

Do not run `shadcn init`. It refuses a project without a Tailwind configuration, and no flag skips
that check. Create `components.json` at your project root instead. This is the file a working pilot
uses:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://ui.shadcn.com/schema.json",
  "style": "new-york",
  "rsc": false,
  "tsx": true,
  "tailwind": { "config": "", "css": "src/index.css", "baseColor": "neutral", "cssVariables": true },
  "aliases": { "components": "@/components", "utils": "@/lib/utils", "ui": "@/components/ui", "lib": "@/lib", "hooks": "@/hooks" },
  "registries": { "@sando-ui": "https://sando-ui.github.io/r/latest/{name}.json" }
}
```

- `registries` is the only line Sando needs. The registry is hosted at `https://sando-ui.github.io`.
  `sando install` rewrites this one address to the version it installs, so an `add` never brings a
  file from another release. Do not edit it afterwards; upgrade instead (§ Upgrading).
- The registry serves three kinds of path. `/r/<version>/` is one release, such as `/r/0.1.0/`,
  and never changes. `/r/latest/` is the newest release, and serves nothing until the first release
  is cut. `/r/next/` is the unreleased work, which changes with every commit to Sando and carries a
  prerelease version such as `0.1.0-dev`. Which one you install is the `--version` flag
  (§ Install units); the path you write here is only the starting point.
- Keep a `tailwind` block: without one the CLI rejects the file as an invalid configuration. No
  Sando item reads it, so `"tailwind": { "css": "", "baseColor": "neutral" }` is enough, and
  `src/index.css` does not have to exist.
- Sando files land at fixed paths under `src/` (`src/components`, `src/blocks`, `src/layouts`,
  `src/styles`) and import each other by relative path, so the aliases do not decide where anything
  goes. Keep them anyway; the CLI expects them.

The CLI resolves `@/*` from your TypeScript config. Declare it with `paths` in the root
`tsconfig.json`, and in `tsconfig.app.json` too if your template splits the config:

```json
{ "compilerOptions": { "paths": { "@/*": ["./src/*"] } } }
```

Leave out `baseUrl`. Older shadcn instructions add it, and TypeScript 7 rejects it with TS5102.
`paths` resolves relative to the config file without it.

## Install the tools

Sando ships two npm packages beside the registry: `@sando-ui/cli` (the `sando` command, which
installs units and checks your repository) and `@sando-ui/eslint-plugin` (the rules it runs over your
screens and CSS). Add both as devDependencies at the exact version of the Sando you install, and the
scripts that run them:

```bash
npm install --save-dev --save-exact @sando-ui/cli@<version> @sando-ui/eslint-plugin@<version>
```

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "sando:install": "sando install",
    "sando:check": "sando check && sando verify",
    "sando:review": "sando review"
  }
}
```

- `<version>` is a release number such as `0.1.0`. The tools and the units are released together
  under one number, and the tools work with any Sando of the same major and minor version.
- `sando:check` is the gate: the static checks, then the renders of every changed screen
  (§ Checking your repository). `sando:review` is an AI design review that reports and never blocks.
- ESLint comes with the CLI as one of its dependencies, so a repository that lints with another
  tool needs no ESLint of its own for the checks.
- `sando verify` renders in Chromium. The CLI brings the browser driver (`playwright-core`) but not
  the browser: run `npx playwright-core install chromium` once per machine. That command is the
  driver's own, so the browser it downloads is the revision the driver expects; a bare
  `npx playwright install chromium` fetches whatever `playwright` version npm resolves, which can
  differ.
- Add `.sando/` to `.gitignore`; the checks write their screenshots and reports there.

> **Before the packages are published.** Until `@sando-ui/cli` and `@sando-ui/eslint-plugin` are on
> npm, you are given the two package tarballs. Commit them under `vendor/sando-ui/`, so every clone
> of your repository finds them, and install them in one command, both at once: the CLI depends on
> the plugin at its exact version, which npm resolves from the second tarball and would otherwise
> look for on the registry and not find.
>
> ```bash
> npm install --save-dev --save-exact vendor/sando-ui/sando-ui-cli-<version>.tgz vendor/sando-ui/sando-ui-eslint-plugin-<version>.tgz
> ```
>
> `package.json` then records each as `file:vendor/sando-ui/<tarball>`. When the packages reach
> npm, install them by version as above and delete `vendor/sando-ui/`. Install the packaged files;
> never point `file:` at a Sando checkout, which resolves ESLint from that checkout instead of from
> your repository.

### Your ESLint config

You do not need one: without it, `sando check` runs Sando's shared ESLint config as shipped. Write
one when you want to run ESLint yourself or add rules of your own. This is the whole file Sando
needs:

```js
// eslint.config.js
import { defineConfig } from 'eslint/config'
import sando from '@sando-ui/eslint-plugin'

export default defineConfig([{ extends: [sando.configs.recommended] }])
```

- The shared config reads `design/product.json` from the directory ESLint runs in, so run ESLint
  and the checks from the repository root.
- Add your own config objects after Sando's in the same array. Do not turn a rule the shared
  config sets off, lower it to a warning or change its options: `sando check` (M2) compares your config with the
  shared one for screens, screen stories and `src/local/`, and blocks on any difference.
- An `eslint-disable` comment for one of Sando's rules says why after `--`
  (`// eslint-disable-next-line sando/screen-imports -- <why>`), or M2 blocks it.

## Install units

Keep the list of units in `design/product.json` and install it with `sando install`, so the
installed set never drifts from the list:

```bash
npm run sando:install                     # the version design/product.json records
npm run sando:install -- --version 0.1.0  # the first install: name the version
```

`--version` takes a release number (`0.1.0`), `latest` or `next`:

- A release number installs that release and pins `components.json` to `/r/<version>/`.
- `latest` installs the newest release and pins the number it resolved to, so the next install
  stays on it.
- `next` installs the unreleased work and pins `/r/next/`. It is the only way to install before the
  first release, while `/r/latest/` serves nothing. The prerelease number it carries works too:
  `--version 0.1.0-dev` reads `/r/next/`, says so, and stops if `next` has moved past it.
- With no `--version`, the install uses the version `design/product.json` records (a recorded
  prerelease installs from `next`), and with none recorded, the version of the CLI.

It installs the brand of your `theme` and every unit in `units` through the shadcn CLI, pins the
registry address, refuses to overwrite a file you changed, and records the version and a fingerprint
of every installed file. The file, its fields and the rest of the standard repository layout are
[design-language.md](design-language.md). To pick a unit, start at
[component-usage.md](component-usage.md), and for Blocks [block-index.md](block-index.md).

Every unit, Block and Layout is an item in the `@sando-ui` namespace, and every brand but the default
is its own item, `brand-<name>`. You can add one directly with `npx shadcn add @sando-ui/<item>`,
but nothing then records it, and `sando check` fails a screen that imports a unit the lock does not
know. Add it to `units` and run `sando install` instead.

A repository that installed Sando before these tools runs `sando install --version <version>` once.
If an installed file differs from that version, the install stops and lists it: a file you edited,
or a sign that you were on another version. Restore your edit, or name the right version; pass
`--accept-overwrite` only for files you mean to replace.

### What an `add` puts in your repo

- **The unit's own files**: `<Name>.tsx` and `<Name>.css`, side by side. The `.tsx` imports its
  `.css` itself, so you never import a unit's stylesheet.
- **Every Sando item it depends on**, resolved by the CLI: other units, Layouts, and shared modules
  such as `src/components/icons.tsx` (which brings `src/styles/icons.css` and imports it the same
  way).
- **The shared styles**, on every install: `src/styles/tokens.css`, `src/styles/reset.css` and the
  default brand sheet under `src/styles/themes/`. A `brand-<name>` item adds its own sheet beside
  it.
- **This guide**, on every install, as `docs/sando/*.md`, with `docs/sando/VERSION` (the Sando
  version installed) and `docs/sando/CHANGELOG.md`. It comes with the shared styles, so a reinstall
  keeps it at the release of the units beside it.
- **npm packages**, installed by the CLI: `react-aria-components` for nearly every unit and
  `lucide-react` for any unit that draws an icon. A few units also need `@internationalized/date`
  (date fields and calendars) or `recharts` (charts); the CLI installs those when you add them.

The shadcn CLI writes nothing outside `src/` and `docs/sando/`, and your `package.json` gains the
packages above. `sando install` also writes `design/sando.lock.json`, the `sando` key of
`design/product.json` and the address in `components.json`. It prints how many items and files it
installed and the address it pinned; it does not wire the sheets into your app, which is the next
section.

## Load the global sheets

The CLI does not wire the shared styles into your app. Import them once, at your entry point,
before anything renders:

```tsx
// src/main.tsx
import './styles/reset.css'
import './styles/tokens.css'
import './styles/themes/<your-brand>.css'   // the default brand's sheet, or the one you installed
import App from './App'
```

- `reset.css` sets box sizing, margins, and the body's font, text colour and background from the
  theme.
- `tokens.css` holds the component tokens and the type role classes. It defines no colour or size
  of its own.
- A **brand sheet** holds every colour, size and type value. `tokens.css` alone paints nothing.
  Each is complete, so import only the one you use: another brand's sheet needs no default sheet
  beside it, and an imported sheet you never select still adds its size to your bundle.

The order between these imports does not matter: every brand sheet is scoped so the result is the
same in any order. Import them before your own CSS so your rules can read the tokens they declare.

## Choose the brand on `<html>`

The default brand sheet applies to `:root` and needs no attribute. Any other brand sheet paints
nothing until you name it on the document root:

```html
<html lang="en" data-brand="<your-brand>">
```

Installing a `brand-<name>` item leaves the default sheet installed beside it; import only the one
you use. Without the attribute that sheet paints nothing, and a page that also imports the default
sheet renders in the default brand's colours and corners instead. The sheet's header comment names
the value to set. It must be on `<html>` and not on a wrapper: overlays portal to `<body>`, and
the root is the only ancestor they share. The other attributes that live there, dark mode included,
are in [theming.md](theming.md).

## Fonts

No `@font-face` ships. A theme names its font families, and the browser uses them only if the user's
device has them installed or you load them. Load the faces your brand names and host them yourself;
until you do, every unit falls back to the system font. Which faces each brand uses and how to load
them: [typefaces.md](typefaces.md).

## Upgrading

Sando ships as numbered releases, and your repository stays on the one it records
(`design/product.json` `sando.version`, `docs/sando/VERSION`) until you move it. Treat every
installed Sando file as read-only.

1. Start from a clean working tree, so the upgrade is one reviewable diff.
2. Move the tools to the new version: the release number goes in both packages, exactly.

   ```bash
   npm install --save-dev --save-exact @sando-ui/cli@<new> @sando-ui/eslint-plugin@<new>
   ```

3. Reinstall at that version. This replaces the units, the sheets and this guide, and re-pins
   `components.json`:

   ```bash
   npm run sando:install -- --version <new>
   ```

4. Read what changed since your version: `git diff docs/sando/CHANGELOG.md` shows exactly the entries
   between the version you were on and the new one. Every entry that needs your edit opens with
   `**Breaking:**` (a removed prop, a renamed token, a changed default). Fix `design/`,
   `src/screens/` and `src/local/` for each one; the changelog is the only place these are listed.
5. Check everything, not only what git says changed:

   ```bash
   npm run sando:check -- --all
   ```

6. Commit the whole upgrade together (the packages, the lock, the reinstalled files,
   `components.json`). To undo it, revert that one commit.

`sando check` tells you when a newer release is out, and whether a Breaking release lies between.
While Sando's major version is 0, a release that breaks something raises the minor version (0.1 to
0.2), and every other release the patch version.

Never edit an installed Sando file. The next install refuses to run over the edit, and `sando check`
reports it. When a unit does not do what you need, follow [missing-units.md](missing-units.md).

Copying files out of the registry by hand, without the shadcn CLI, is not supported.

## For your coding agent

Paste this into your repo's `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`. The `docs/sando/` paths are where the CLI
installs the guide; the `design/` and `src/` paths are the standard layout in
[design-language.md](design-language.md):

```markdown
## Sando UI

UI units under src/components, src/blocks and src/layouts, the sheets under src/styles and the
guide under docs/sando are installed from the Sando UI registry by `npm run sando:install`. Never
edit them.
Before writing UI, read the Sando guide in docs/sando/ and follow it:

- styling-contract.md: how your own CSS reads Sando tokens; your own class prefix, never `sd-`
- composition-contract.md: composing units into screens, icons, the accessibility you owe
- spacing-contract.md: which space token goes between which things
- prop-usage-contract.md: which size and variant to pass
- component-usage.md and block-index.md: which unit to use
- missing-units.md: what to do when Sando has no unit for the job
- theming.md: the attributes on <html>

### Building a screen

This repo keeps its design in design/, laid out as docs/sando/design-language.md defines. To
build or change a screen, read in this order, each narrowing the one before and never overriding it:

1. the Sando guide above;
2. design/DESIGN.md: what the service is, who uses it, its UX policy and design language;
3. the screen's entry in design/SCREENS.md: purpose, section stack, states and verbatim copy,
   and the flows in its § Flows that pass through the screen. No entry yet: write it first and
   have it confirmed; never invent anatomy or copy;
4. design/product.json: the compose and usage rules and the policy for each unit you place,
   its contexts and lang. Every Sando unit a file under src/screens/ imports is in its `units`
   list, even one another listed unit already brings; anything else comes from src/local/;
5. docs/sando/missing-units.md, when no installed unit renders what the entry needs.

Screens go in src/screens/, one file per SCREENS.md entry; units this repo owns go in src/local/.
A screen is pure: it renders from its props alone, with no fetching, storage, URL access, clock,
randomness or effects; that code goes in the route layer (src/app/ unless the framework has its
own). Each screen has src/screens/<Name>.stories.tsx with a `Default` story and one story per state
in its N.3 (docs/sando/design-language.md § Screens and service logic). After adding a unit to
design/product.json, run `npm run sando:install`.

Before you call a screen finished, run `npm run sando:check` (`sando check`, then `sando verify`)
and fix every blocking finding. Then open the screenshots under .sando/verify/screens/<Name>/ and
look at them against the SCREENS.md entry: a passing report does not show you a wrong layout.
`npm run sando:review -- <Name>` adds a design review; it reports and never blocks. When a review
finds a defect in a screen, fix it and record it as docs/sando/design-language.md § A finding
becomes a rule says: shared defects go upstream to Sando, service-specific ones into design/.
```

## Checking your repository

Three commands check a service against this guide. Each prints its findings and exits 1 when a
blocking one remains. `sando check` prints its own findings by id and an ESLint finding by its rule
name; the table gives both.

| Command | When | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `sando check` | every commit and in CI | the layout files, screens and stories, the installed files and versions, your ESLint config, and the ESLint rules over your own files under `src/` (every path but the installed ones) |
| `sando verify [Screen...]` | after changing a screen, and in CI with `--all` | renders every screen in every story, at 390, at each breakpoint step and at 1280, in each colour scheme `policy.render.schemes` names (default light and dark), theme and usage context, with the clock, time zone and language fixed; writes `.sando/verify/` |
| `sando review <Name>` | when a screen is built or changed | an AI design review of one screen against its `SCREENS.md` entry, `DESIGN.md` Part 2 and its screenshots; runs `claude` (or `codex` with `--runner codex`); with neither on your `PATH` it writes the evidence and prompt to `.sando/review/<Name>/` for any AI you choose; report only |

   renders only the changed screens. Now `sando:check` can run in CI.

   `sando verify --baseline-prune` lower the counts; nothing raises them. `sando verify` lowers only
   the counts of the screens it rendered, so prune after a run that covered them, or with `--all`.
5. When every count in a file is 0, delete it.

and the page attributes (R3) are never baselined.

```bash
npm run sando:check -- --all
```
