# Missing units: when Sando has no unit for what you need

What to do when a screen in your repository needs a Component or a Block that Sando does not ship:
whether the unit belongs in Sando or in your repository, how to build a local bridge that does not
fight the units around it, how to ask for the unit upstream, and why you never edit the Sando files
you installed. Read it before writing any UI that is not a composition of installed Sando units.

Hand-maintained; no check reads this file.

## Is it Sando's or yours

One question decides it: **will another product use it?**

| What you need | Where it is made |
|---|---|
| A Component (a control, a field, an indicator, anything with behaviour or a look of its own) | **Always in Sando.** Components are never built in a consumer repository, not even temporarily as a fork. |
| A Block that two or more products would use (a card shape, a list row, a sheet, a toolbar) | **In Sando.** Ask for it upstream (§ Asking upstream) and bridge it locally until it ships. |
| A composition that only your product has (its own hero, a one-off arrangement of installed units, a page section no other service would want) | **In your repository**, by the rules below. |

When the answer is unclear, treat it as Sando's. A local unit that turns out to be shared costs a
second implementation and a migration; a request that turns out to be product-only costs one reply.

## Building it locally

A local unit, whether it is a temporary bridge for a Sando unit or a composition your product owns,
follows the same rules as the code around it:

- **Compose installed Sando units.** Reach for a Layout (`Stack`, `Grid`, `Container`) and the
  Components you already have before writing an element of your own. How to compose is
  [`composition-contract.md`](composition-contract.md).
- **Style with Sys tokens only.** Never a Cmp token (`--sd-<component>-*`, which is Sando's internal
  implementation and may change in any release), never a Ref token, and never a literal for a value a
  shared scale already carries (space, radius, colour, type, layer, breakpoint). The full rule is
  [`styling-contract.md`](styling-contract.md).
- **Use your own class prefix, never `sd-`.** Keep every bridge class under one prefix of your own;
  the rule and its examples are [`styling-contract.md`](styling-contract.md) § Your own class prefix,
  never `sd-`.
- **Never style a unit's internal classes.** A part class (`.sd-<unit>__<part>`) or a child selector
  into a unit is that unit's implementation, not its API, and a reinstall changes it without notice.
  If the unit cannot do what you need through its props, that is a gap to raise, not a selector to
  write.

A bridge for a unit Sando will ship has three more rules, because its job is to be deleted:

- **Shape it like the unit it stands in for.** Give it the name, props and composition the Sando unit
  is likely to have (a `Text` with a `tone`, a `Figure` with a `caption`), so the day Sando ships the
  unit your screens change an import and nothing else.
- **Keep every bridge in one file and one stylesheet**, each export numbered against your list of
  gaps (G1, G2, ...), so the list and the code cannot drift apart. Nothing outside that pair styles
  the bridges.
- **Delete it when Sando ships the unit.** Install the Sando unit, switch the import, remove the
  export and its styles, and strike the gap from your list. A bridge that outlives its unit is a
  second implementation of a Sando unit, which is the one thing this page exists to prevent.

## Never edit installed Sando files

The files an install writes into your repository belong to Sando. **Do not edit them**, however
small the change: the next reinstall overwrites the edit, or conflicts with it, and either way the
fix is lost. A forked copy also stops receiving accessibility and behaviour fixes. `sando install`
records a fingerprint of every installed file, and `sando check` fails on any file that no longer
matches it ([getting-started.md](getting-started.md) § Checking your repository, U6).

When an installed unit does not do what you need, in this order:

1. **Use its props.** Most needs are a `size`, a `variant`, a slot or a composition the unit already
   offers.
2. **Compose around it.** Wrap it in a Layout, place it in a Block, pass a different child.
3. **Fix it in Sando and reinstall.** Ask for the change upstream (below); when it ships, reinstall
   the unit and take the new version.

A local bridge (§ Building it locally) is how you keep working between step 3's request and its
release. It sits beside the installed files, never inside them.

## Asking upstream

Open an issue on the Sando repository for every Component, and for every Block another product would
use. A request that gets built quickly says:

- **The pattern, as a role.** What the unit is for and where it appears on your screens, in words a
  second product could recognise ("a checklist row with a yes or no status chip"), not your
  product's copy.
- **What you tried.** The installed units and props you composed, and the point where they could not
  carry it.
- **Your bridge, if you built one.** Its props show the shape you need; Sando may ship a different
  one, and your bridge then follows Sando's.

Keep a running list of open gaps in your product's design language (see
[`design-language.md`](design-language.md) § 8. Which unit renders each pattern), one row per pattern
with no unit yet, so the requests and the bridges have one place to be counted.

# Prop Usage Contract: which size and which variant, by position

One-line scope: **which `size` and `variant` a Block, Screen or studio panel passes to a Component.**
It loads on all three because the laws bind all three, and they bind your own screens the same way.
How Blocks and Screens are composed otherwise is [`composition-contract.md`](composition-contract.md).

A Block, Screen or studio panel picks a Component's `size` and `variant` by the element's
**position**, never by taste, and `prop-usage:check` holds every site to the POSITION laws below
(every size law; the ladder, strong, media, wordless and surface variant laws). The destructive, tonal, badge and
valence laws are MEANING, and review holds them; so is the canvas law, because what is painted under
a Button is CSS that the JSX does not show. Where the
structure cannot say, a comment before the element declares the law it follows,
`{/* usage: item-action: why */}`, and an unknown word fails. The words are `chrome`, `item-action` and `completing-action`. Derived from classifying all 216
sized and 190 variant sites in Sando on 2026-09-25.

**Size.** The default (`medium`, the prop omitted) unless a row below names another.

| Law | Tell it by structure | Size |
|---|---|---|
| **default** | anything no row below names: fields, a field's own action, a card-grid or empty-state call to action, a content toolbar over its collection | omit `size`. `large` is never spent for emphasis on a control-height control, since prominence between siblings is the variant's job |
| **completing-action** | the action row that ENDS its unit: a form's submit and the Buttons sharing its row or `ButtonGroup` (no field in that row), a Dialog or Drawer footer, the `actions` of a page-opening `Hero` or `CtaSection` | `large`. Size here marks the unit's level in the page's hierarchy, not emphasis among siblings, which is still the variant's (owner, 2026-09-30). A submit that is its field's own action (in a row with it, or directly under a lone field, as a comment composer) stays at the field's size; a reset, a filter, or a list of alternatives such as `ActionSheet` is not a completion |
| **row** | control-height controls sharing one row (a `direction="row"` Stack at any canvas, a Toolbar, a Block's actions slot drawn in a row) | ONE size across the row, so the boxes and their focus-ring band align; the row takes the size another law gives its field or bar |
| **chrome** | a control owned by a BAR (a root drawn as `header`, `nav` or `role="toolbar"`, a Card holding one row of controls, a card's icon-and-count reaction row), a control passed through a prop that a Layout or Block renders whole inside a `header` or `nav` (AppShell's `navTrigger` and `header`), a Block whose root is one trigger Button meant for a bar slot, or a control overlaid on a media tile. Not a DESTINATION (a component with `isCurrent`, a NavItem): a nav's destinations are what the bar is made of, so they take the default, and a denser nav passes its own `size` (owner, 2026-10-29). Not a PICKER either (FieldButton): it shows the value the page is filtered or sorted by, so it takes the default in a bar and may still go `small` where a row law asks (owner, 2026-11-02) | `small` |
| **item-action** | a control acting on ONE item of a repeated collection: rendered per item of a list, card stack, table or grid list (a `.map()` or a collection's render prop), including an inline value it edits, or inside the Alert it answers | `small`. A card GRID's call to action is **default** |
| **workshop** | a control-height control under `src/studio/**` | `medium`, the size omitted, in the panels and the bars alike: one control height across both studios (owner, 2026-10-29). It outranks **completing-action**, so a studio Dialog's footer stays `medium` too; `prop-usage:check` applies the completion law outside `src/studio` only |
| **surface** | a `Card` | default; `small` only when it IS a bar (one row of controls) or an empty specimen of the surface |
| **painted-box** | an `Avatar` or `ColorSwatch` | `small` beside a line of text, packed in a cluster or inside a control; `large` Avatar / `medium` swatch when it is the one subject of its unit (above its own name, beside its own controls) |

An `isMediaOnly` Button's size is the extent of the media it frames and is outside these laws.

**Variant.** Emphasis and intent, never a palette role.

| Law | Tell it by structure | Variant |
|---|---|---|
| **ladder** | the Buttons of one action group (siblings in a row Stack, a `ButtonGroup`, a Dialog/Drawer footer, one form) | at most ONE `primary`, the group's forward action (it completes or advances the task: submit, confirm, next, the page's call to action), and last in a `ButtonGroup`. Every other worded Button is `secondary`, the non-primary rung, whose look the BRAND decides (a neutral fill or an outline); `surface` where the canvas law applies. An action rendered per item of a collection is never `primary` |
| **tonal** | a non-primary action that still advances the task by another path (apply a discount, split a payment) | `tonal`, medium emphasis on the brand's tint. Never the forward action, which is `primary` |
| **strong** | an action co-equal with the forward one but not the brand's call: the declining half of a two-way choice, a set of equal tool actions beside a cart | `strong`, the neutral solid. Never the only Button of its group |
| **media** | a Button overlaid on a photo, video or media tile, or one that frames media (`isMediaOnly`) | `outline`, whose transparent fill frosts what sits behind it. Never a ladder rung: on a surface it is `secondary` |
| **wordless** | a Button showing no word: icon-only, a drag handle, a glyph with its count | `ghost` in chrome or on a painted row; a Button with a word is never `ghost` |
| **canvas** | a Button whose rung would be `secondary`, sitting on a canvas that is not a surface: a tinted row, a grey canvas, a wallpaper | `surface`, the page's own surface and ink. Never on the page's own surface, where it has no edge or fill to tell it apart. |
| **destructive** | the one press that commits a loss the UI cannot restore, or opens its confirmation | `destructive`. Removing what the user can add back the same way is `secondary` |
| **provider** | a Button that hands the action to a third party (sign in, share or subscribe through another service) | `provider`, with the party's colour pair; several providers are peers, so the one-`primary` rule does not rank them |
| **badge** | a Badge | by what it states: `neutral` a count, tag or plain state; `error` a failure to act on; `success` a completed state (Paid, Done); `warning` a state at risk or still needing action (Low stock); `info` a notice that is neither (Beta, Coming soon); `tonal` the one promotional or attention item (Popular, an unread count); `primary` the brand solid, only for a count nested inside a Button (Filter 3) or a recommendation ribbon over a tile, since beside a Button the attention chip is `tonal`; `strong` a state stamped over the item that stops it (Sold out); `category` one member of a set told apart by colour (a sales channel), never a valence; a metric's change is `neutral`, or `error` when its data marks it bad news, and its direction is an arrow, never a colour (falling refunds is good); `overlay` a readable label over media, using inverse backing and ink; `live` a thing happening now (a stream, a session in progress), never a failure. `urgency` a reason to act now with no status attached (a deal ending, a discount rate), never a failure, which is `error`. One fact takes its valence once: beside an `error` Badge that carries a failure, its summary stays `neutral` |
| **valence** | an `Alert`, `Toast` or `Meter` (a Meter has no `info`; its neutral is `standard`) | how the content is judged, never how urgent: `neutral` a note that judges nothing and asks no attention (an Alert or Banner only: a promotion line, a device notice), `error` a failed attempt, `success` a completed one, `warning` done but still needing the reader's action or at risk, `info` a notice; urgency is Alert's `live` |
| **surface** | a `Card`; a `Link` | `Card` is `flat` unless it floats over content (fixed or sticky); `raised` then. A `Link` standing as an item in a set of links (nav, footer, sub-nav, contents) is `quiet`; inside prose it is `standard` |
| **data** | a variant expression or a forwarded prop | legitimate when every branch passes the law a literal of that value would, and a forwarded prop is typed to the same union and defaulted by the same law |

**Ratio.** An `AspectRatio` around a picture that IS the content takes one rung of one ladder:
`1` (thumbnails, avatars, symbol and category tiles, gallery tiles) · `4 / 3` (a product or device
render on its well) · `3 / 2` (a photograph) · `16 / 9` (video, a screen capture) · `2` (a banner or
an article thumbnail), and `3 / 4` or `2 / 3` for the same pictures stood upright. A ratio is never
fitted to one asset's pixels (`268 / 184` is `3 / 2`). A decorative well holding an icon takes no
`AspectRatio`: its height is the icon's plus its padding, so widening its card cannot flatten it. A
row or grid of logos puts every mark in ONE box, `5` for wordmarks and `1` for symbols, the mark
`contain`ed inside, so marks of different shapes read as one even row; a bare height is not a box.
Derived from every `ratio` passed in the repo on 2026-11-02 (`1` ×4, `4 / 3` ×3, `16 / 9` ×3, `2`
×1, one fitted literal) and a measured reference service's media. Review holds it.

**Lines.** A line that parts content (a `Separator` between sections or rows, a rule inside a card)
is `isDecorative`: `border.decorative`, which WCAG 1.4.11 does not cover. The functional
`border.DEFAULT` belongs to the edge of a control the user operates (a field, a checkbox, an outline
chip), where 3:1 is owed. A dark line between two paragraphs is this law broken. Review holds it.

**Fill.** A picture inside `AspectRatio` fills the box (`inline-size` and `block-size` 100%) with its
`object-fit` stated: `cover` for a photograph, `contain` for a cut-out on a well. A picture left at
its natural size inside a ratio box is a crop nobody chose.

**Content.** A count or amount inside a Button comes AFTER the label it counts ("Cart 3", "Pay ₩12,000"),
so a row of such buttons scans by its words. `prop-usage:check` holds a number-typed value in the
Button's own JSX; a count already formatted into a label prop is review.

# Shared classes and the base stylesheet

The Sando classes your own markup may carry, and what the installed base stylesheet does to your
page before any unit renders. Everything here ships in the `styles` item: the type-role classes in
`src/styles/tokens.css`, the rest in `src/styles/reset.css`. No other `sd-` class is yours to use;
why is [`styling-contract.md`](styling-contract.md).

Hand-maintained; no check reads this file. The installed stylesheets are the authority: if a class
named here is missing from them, or one there is missing here, the stylesheet is right.

## The classes

| Class | Lives in | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| `.sd-type-<role>-<size>` | `tokens.css` | One type role applied whole: family where the role has its own face, size, weight, line height and tracking, as one set. |
| `.sd-type-<role>-<size>-emphasized` | `tokens.css` | The same role one weight rung heavier, with the same size, line height and tracking. |
| `.sd-visually-hidden` | `reset.css` | Hides content from sight and keeps it in the accessibility tree: a label a screen reader needs and the layout does not show. |
| `.sd-tabular` | `reset.css` | Tabular figures, so digits line up in columns (a table cell, a price column, a countdown). On or off, no scale. Pair it with a type role. |

## Type roles

Eight roles, three sizes each, and an emphasized twin of every one: 48 classes. The roles are
`display`, `headline`, `title`, `subtitle`, `body`, `label`, `caption` and `code`; `display` and
`headline` draw in the brand's display face and `code` in its mono face. Which role a text takes,
and which size, is [`styling-contract.md`](styling-contract.md) § Type comes whole, from a role.

Sizes are `small`, `medium` and `large`, so a class reads `sd-type-body-medium` or
`sd-type-title-small-emphasized`. A type size is not a unit's `size` prop; the two coincide often
and are unrelated.

**Reach for `Text` first.** The `Text` component renders the same classes from props (`variant`,
`size`, `isEmphasized`) and adds a colour `tone`. Use a class directly where `Text` cannot go: a
`strong` or `em` inside a line, which takes the emphasized twin of the line it sits in so its weight
is the same in every brand, or an element of your own that must be something `Text` does not
render.

**Every type class also indents its text.** Each one carries a padding at zero specificity on both
inline sides, one `--sd-text-inset-inline` wide, so text stands just inside the rounded box around it.
Two things follow:

- Put the class on the text, never on a box that only lends its font to what is inside. If you must,
  give that box `padding-inline: 0` in your own class, so the boxes inside stay on the line.
- Your own class wins whenever it sets inline padding, because the inset carries no weight. If your
  element sets its own `padding-inline`, that value must hold the inset itself.

## `.sd-visually-hidden`

For text a screen reader must hear and the screen must not show: the name of an icon-only control
you built, a table caption, a hint after a visual cue. It stays focusable if the element is. Do not
use it to hide content from everyone; that is the `hidden` attribute, or `Show` for a width-dependent
copy.

## What `reset.css` does to your page

The base stylesheet is small, and each rule is one you would otherwise write:

- **Box sizing.** Every element and pseudo-element uses `border-box`.
- **Margins.** Every element's default margin is zero. Spacing comes from the layout, never from a
  browser default.
- **The page itself.** `body` is at least the viewport's height and takes the Sys font family, the
  default text ink and the canvas background, so a page with no units on it already reads in the
  theme.
- **Form controls inherit type.** `button`, `input`, `select` and `textarea` inherit font and colour.
  Without this a browser draws them in its own font, which is why a Sando control pasted into a page
  without `reset.css` shows the wrong face.
- **Text selection** is drawn in the theme's selection pair.
- **An inverse ground re-inks itself.** An element with `data-ground="inverse"` swaps every colour
  role in its subtree to the opposite theme, and its text colour follows. What the attribute is
  for is [`theming.md`](theming.md).
- **Korean wraps between words.** Under `:lang(ko)`, lines break at spaces rather than between
  syllables, and a long run with no space still wraps. It applies only where the language is
  declared, so a Korean page sets `<html lang="ko">`, or `lang="ko"` on the element.

Which stylesheets to import, and in what order, is [`getting-started.md`](getting-started.md).

# Spacing Contract: which gap goes between two things

This file decides the space you put between units in your own code: the `gap` you pass a `Stack` or
`Grid`, and any `gap`, `padding` or `margin` in your own CSS. Every answer is a RUNG of a Sando
scale, never a pixel value, because the pixels differ from one theme to another and between the
`small` and `medium` breakpoints while the rungs keep their order.

Not enforced in your repository. Nothing reads your spacing choices; this file and review are what
hold them.

The `space` rungs, tightest first: `none` · `2x-small` · `x-small` · `small` · `medium` · `large` ·
`x-large` · `2x-large`. A `Stack` or `Grid` `gap` takes these words; in your own CSS they are
`var(--sd-space-<rung>)`, and `none` is `0`. "Two rungs looser" below means two steps along this
line: `x-small` to `medium`, `small` to `large`.

## Family first

- **`space` is the fallback, not the first choice.** When a purpose family fits, it wins even where
  the value happens to be the same:
  - a container's own interior padding takes `var(--sd-surface-padding-<size>)`;
  - the page frame's side margin takes `var(--sd-grid-margin)`;
  - a bar or panel floating over the viewport keeps `var(--sd-overlay-margin-medium)` from its edge.

  The values coincide in some themes and not in others, so a value that looks right is no evidence
  the family is.
- **A box built to be pressed takes `control-height`; a square sized by what it holds takes
  `size`.** Use `var(--sd-control-height-<size>)` for something with the height of a control,
  named like the control's own `size`; use `var(--sd-size-<size>)` for a plate around a glyph or a
  picture. The two scales share some values, so the number cannot tell you which you picked.
- **Read `layer` and `duration` by name, never by value.** The order is what the token carries;
  the number behind it is an implementation detail.

## Two laws, and the edge

Every gap answers one question first: **does one side name or act on the other?**

- **Parting (no, they do not belong to each other).** The gap between two units is at least **two
  rungs looser** than the loosest gap inside either of them on the same axis. Equal fails; one rung
  looser fails too. Read it on the ink: a control's own inner padding at a unit's edge adds to the
  gap it sits on.
- **Attachment (yes: a head over what it names, or actions after what they act on).** A heading,
  label, eyebrow or byline above its content, or the buttons after a form, sits **at least** at the
  loosest same-axis gap G inside either side, never tighter, or the head reads as one of the members.
  What caps it is the parting law one level out: the gap OUTSIDE the attached unit must be two rungs
  looser than the attachment gap. A head drifting loose shows up as that outer gap failing.
- **An edge is a step.** Across something drawn (a `Card`'s border, a `Separator` between every
  pair, a painted fill, an image) the gap may equal the inner gap, never less; the edge does the rest
  of the parting. The edge also seals the unit: no gap behind it is compared with a gap outside it.

A nested Layout at the same gap as its siblings, holding the same kind of unit they are (Blocks among
Blocks, Components among Components), is one rhythm with them, not a new level.

## Common relationships

Where a row says **floor**, a looser rung is allowed; where it names a rung, use that rung.

**Parting**

| Relationship | Rung |
|---|---|
| **field-field**: labelled fields stacked in a column | `medium`. With a `Slider` among them, two rungs over the Slider's own size: `medium`, `large`, `x-large` for a `small`, `medium`, `large` Slider. The options of ONE choice are not fields: use `CheckboxGroup` or `RadioGroup`, which own that gap |
| **stacked-units**: items or regions in one column, parted only by air (no Card, no row padding, no Separator) | floor: two rungs over the loosest gap inside any of them (`2x-small` inside gives `small`, `x-small` gives `medium`, `small` gives `large`, `medium` gives `x-large`, `large` gives `2x-large`). Units with no inner gap: floor `2x-small`. One child: `none` |
| **page**: the Blocks of a Screen, and any Layout that only arranges them | two rungs over the loosest top-level gap among ALL its Blocks, one value on both axes, however you nest Stack and Grid |
| **spread-regions**: the two ends of a bar or row pushed apart (`justify="between"`) | floor: two rungs over a region's own gap; `small` when neither region has one |
| **leaf-row**: a row of peer leaves that are not actions (chips, thumbnails, links, logos, nav destinations, stat cells) | `x-small` between separately painted items, `medium` between unpainted text links, floor `small` between logos, nav destinations and chart columns |
| **separator-rows**: rows with a `Separator` between each pair | floor: the rows' own inner gap, at least `2x-small` |
| **padded-rows**: rows whose own box carries block padding (a padded list row, a `NavItem`) | floor `none`: the padding, counted twice, is the parting |
| **card-grid**: a `Grid` of bordered `Card`s | `medium`. The border is the delimiter, so less air is needed |
| **card-stack**: one column of full-width bordered `Card`s | `small` |
| **bar-groups**: two groups of DIFFERENT function inside one `Toolbar` | a vertical `ToolbarSeparator` between them, placed straight in the Toolbar beside the groups, never inside a gapped `Stack` (the Stack's gap would add to the separator's own inset). Groups of the same function stay one action-row |
| **link-list**: a stack of bare single-line links | floor `x-small`, so each link plus its gap reaches the minimum target size |

**Attachment**

| Relationship | Rung |
|---|---|
| **pair**: a head line over its own support line (title over description, name over meta, label over value) | `2x-small` when the pair is the only child of its column or the support line is a figure; `x-small` when a sibling shares the column, or when the head is a row that wraps (a title with its Badges) |
| **heading-group**: a heading above the one box it heads, including a form's `h1` over its fields | see [The gap under a heading](#the-gap-under-a-heading) |
| **actions**: the actions after the content they act on, or the controls before it (a form's submit, a banner's buttons, a search field or toolbar over its list) | floor G. A form whose fields sit at `medium` takes `large` for its heading and its submit |
| **field-with-action**: one field beside its button, nothing between (stacked above it below `medium`) | `small` |
| **text-and-control**: a text column, value or preview beside the ONE control or cluster that acts on it | `small` |
| **inline-media**: an `Avatar` or media box beside a text column | `small` |
| **heading-badge**: Badges packed after the heading they annotate | `x-small`, which also serves badge to badge |
| **action-row**: peer pressables packed in one row or column | `x-small` between Buttons that paint a resting fill; `none` between the transparent toggles of one choice, so the selected fill reads as one segment |
| **bridged-sequence**: items whose own drawing reaches the neighbour (a connector line, an overlap) | `none`; any gap cuts the line |

**Insets are not gaps between units**, and each has its own answer: an unpainted section root's edge
inset takes floor `small` and stays under the surface padding of a `Card` it wraps; a page-opening or
closing band takes `2x-large` block padding; a self-contained page section is framed by the grid
margin inline and `medium` block; room reserved for something that is not a sibling (list markers,
a scrollbar, a unit suffix) is the size of what it reserves.

A relationship that none of these rows names still answers to one of the two laws or the edge. Decide
which, then apply it.

## The gap under a heading

A heading is ATTACHED to the box it heads, so its gap is at least that box's own inner gap G, and
what bounds it from above is the gap outside the whole unit, which must part it by two rungs.

- G is `none` (a flush collection under the heading): `medium`.
- The options under the heading sit in ONE row: `x-small`, and their wrapped rows take that rung too.
- A heading directly over its own support line is the **pair** row, not this one.
- **A heading placed directly AMONG peer items** that have no box of their own takes the items' gap.
  The fix is to nest the items in their own `Stack`, never to pick a special rung for the heading.

There is no rung per heading role. A `title` heading and a `label` heading over the same box take
the same gap; the box decides.

```tsx
<Stack gap="x-large">              {/* parting: section from section */}
  <Stack gap="medium">             {/* attachment: heading at G */}
    <Text variant="title" elementType="h2">Notifications</Text>
    <Stack gap="medium">           {/* field-field */}
      <Switch>Email</Switch>
      <Switch>Push</Switch>
    </Stack>
  </Stack>
  <Stack gap="medium">
    <Text variant="title" elementType="h2">Privacy</Text>
    ...
  </Stack>
</Stack>
```

## A flex gap is handed to every child

A gap is spent on the relationship it NAMES, and a flex or grid `gap` lands between EVERY pair of
children. Put the gap that parts one section from the next on a section's own flex container and it
also lands between that section's header and the rows the header labels, so the header sits nearer
the group above it than the rows below. Nest instead: the outer container parts the sections, and
each section has its own container for its header and rows. A section's rows are parted by whatever
parts the rows of a list with no header.

# Styling contract: the CSS you write beside installed Sando units

This file governs every stylesheet you write in your own repository next to the Sando units you
installed: a page's layout, a local bridge for a unit Sando does not ship yet, a product-only
composition. It settles which tokens that CSS may read, which values it may never write as
literals, which class names are yours, and which selectors are off limits. The installed Sando files
themselves are not yours to style or edit; [`missing-units.md`](missing-units.md) says what to do
when one of them falls short.

Not enforced by a script in your repository. Sando checks its own stylesheets; nothing it installs
checks yours, so this file is the whole of the guard.

## Why this exists

A consumer repository that vendored Sando units in October 2026, before this guide existed, wrote
correct Sys-token CSS under its own prefix and still broke in five ways. It pinned `AppShell`'s
header with a child selector into the unit (`> .sd-app-shell__header`) and a bare `z-index: 2`. It
sized a page with `100vh`. It wrote `768px` into three media queries. It rebuilt the theme selector
cascade by hand to flip an image in dark mode. And it leaned on Sando classes no consumer document
named. Every one of those is answered below, and every one was already forbidden inside Sando, in
files the consumer never received.

## Read Sys tokens, never Cmp or Ref

Sando's tokens come in three tiers, and your CSS reads exactly one of them.

| Tier | Looks like | Where it lives once installed | Yours to read? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sys**, purpose | `--sd-color-text-muted`, `--sd-space-medium`, `--sd-radius-large`, `--sd-layer-sticky` | the brand sheet, `src/styles/themes/<brand>.css`, every name that does not start `--sd-ref-` | **Yes, and only these.** |
| **Cmp**, one unit's hook | `--sd-button-*`, `--sd-app-shell-*`, `--sd-color-swatch-*` | `src/styles/tokens.css`, every custom property in its `:root` | **No.** |
| **Ref**, the raw value | `--sd-ref-*` | the brand sheet | **No.** |

- **Sys is the only tier with a promise.** Every brand ships the same Sys names, so a Sys reference
  keeps working when the product switches theme. A Sys token names a purpose, and the theme decides
  the value.
- **Cmp is a unit's implementation.** It is renamed, split or removed when the unit changes, with no
  notice to you. Reading `--sd-button-padding-inline` to line something up with a Button couples
  your CSS to Button's internals as surely as a child selector would.
- **Ref is named by its value, so its names differ per brand.** A border rung one brand calls by one
  number, another brand calls by a different one. A Ref name that resolves today is absent from the
  next theme, and the declaration silently falls back to nothing.
- **Tell the tiers apart by file, not by name.** `--sd-color-swatch-size-small` reads like a Sys
  colour and is a Cmp token of the ColorSwatch unit. If a name is in `tokens.css`, it is Cmp.

The Sys families you will reach for most: colour (`text`, `icon`, `background`, `surface`, `fill`,
`border`, `selection`, `chart`), `space`, `control-height`, `radius`, `border` (line widths),
`layer`, `shadow`, `duration` and `easing`, and `state` (hover, pressed, focus ring, disabled). The
brand sheet is the complete list. What the colour families mean, in one line each:

- `background` is the canvas plane only: the page, a section backdrop, a scrim. A control is never
  painted with it.
- `surface` is neutral paper that holds content (a card, an overlay); `surface-inset` is the field a
  control sits in.
- `fill` is colour deliberately applied to a foreground element: a solid action, a status chip, a
  subtle tint.
- `text` and `icon` are ink. An `on-*` ink belongs to the solid fill it sits on and is read only on
  that fill.
- `border` is a line.

## Never write a literal for a value a scale carries

If a Sys family holds the value, a literal is a fork of it: it misses the next theme, the dark
mode, and the mobile step that some rungs take. Colour, spacing, radius, line width, type, stacking
and timing all have a family. Three literals look harmless and are not:

- **Stacking.** Chrome pinned to the viewport (a sticky header, a fixed bottom bar) takes
  `z-index: var(--sd-layer-sticky)`. The `layer` family is an order, read by name, never by
  magnitude. A small literal is fine in one case only: ordering siblings inside your own local unit,
  where it means nothing outside it.

  ```css
  /* No: a bare number deciding what clears another unit. */
  .app-header { position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 2; }
  ```

  ```css
  /* Yes. */
  .app-header { position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: var(--sd-layer-sticky); }
  ```

- **The viewport's height.** A page that fills the screen is a Layout's job: `<Layer isFullHeight>`
  already sizes to the dynamic viewport, which leaves no gap under a phone's browser bar. A
  hand-written `100vh` duplicates that and loses the fix, because `vh` measures the largest
  viewport and the bar covers the bottom of it.
- **Breakpoints.** Do not write a width of your own in `@media` or `matchMedia`. Layout primitives
  take a responsive value (`direction={{ small: "column", medium: "row" }}`), and `Show`
  (`from="large"`, `below="large"`) places one control in two spots by width without any script.
  When a stylesheet truly needs a media query, it uses one of the ladder's widths and nothing else.
  The ladder and its names are in [`composition-contract.md`](composition-contract.md) § Responsive, mobile first.

A value that is not on any scale stays a literal: `0`, `100%`, `1fr`, `display: grid`. The test is
whether a Sys family names the thing, not whether the declaration has a number in it.

## Your own class prefix, never `sd-`

Every class you write carries a prefix of your own: `app-`, or `<app>g-` for gap bridges, or any
short word that is yours. `sd-` belongs to Sando. A local `.sd-figure` collides the day Sando ships a
Figure, and from then on two stylesheets fight over one class with nothing to tell you which wins.
The same holds for custom properties: a local one is `--app-*`, never `--sd-*`.

## One class per element, no reaching into a unit

- **One class, low specificity.** Style an element through its own class. No descendant
  combinators (`.app-card .app-title`); give the title its own class instead. An attribute on the
  same element is fine (`.app-tile[data-selected]`).
- **Never target a unit's internals.** A part class (`.sd-<unit>__<part>`), a unit's root class
  (`.sd-select`, `.sd-button`) and a child selector into a unit are its implementation, not its API.
  A reinstall renames them without notice. The same goes for restyling a unit through the `data-*`
  state it emits.

  ```css
  /* No: restyling AppShell from outside. */
  .app-shell > .sd-app-shell__header { position: sticky; top: 0; }
  ```

  To change how a unit looks, use its props: `variant`, `size`, a slot, a different child. If no
  prop does it, the unit has a gap, and a gap is a request upstream plus, meanwhile, a local bridge
  ([`missing-units.md`](missing-units.md)), never a selector. `AppShell` has no sticky-header prop
  today, so the selector above is that request, unwritten.
- **Your `className` on a unit places it; it does not restyle it.** Margin, grid placement,
  `align-self` and width in a layout are yours. Colour, border, radius, padding and type inside the
  unit are the unit's.

## State on your own elements reads `data-*`

When you build a local element on a React Aria primitive, style its states with the attributes React
Aria emits, on the same element: `[data-hovered]`, `[data-pressed]`, `[data-focus-visible]`,
`[data-selected]`, `[data-disabled]`, `[data-invalid]`, and whatever else that primitive emits. Never
mirror a state into a class of your own, and never write `:hover` where React Aria emits
`data-hovered`.
Draw a focus ring from the `state` family (`--sd-state-focus-ring`, `--sd-state-focus-ring-width`,
`--sd-state-focus-ring-opacity`), so it matches every Sando unit beside it.

## The theme is already in the token

A Sys colour swaps on its own for dark mode, the brand, an inverse ground, and a contrast mode where
the theme ships one. Your
CSS never tests the theme itself:

```css
/* No: a hand-built copy of the theme cascade. */
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) .app-logo { filter: invert(1); } }
:root[data-theme="dark"] .app-logo { filter: invert(1); }
```

That copy is already wrong in a way that is hard to see: it ignores an inverse ground
(`data-ground="inverse"`), where the colours flip back, so the logo inverts on a ground that is light
again. Read a Sys role and every one of those cases comes free. If no role covers what you need, as
with an image that must follow the scheme, that is a gap ([`missing-units.md`](missing-units.md)).
What the theme attributes are and where they go is [`theming.md`](theming.md).

## Type comes whole, from a role

- **Write text through `Text`**, which takes a role (`variant`), a `size`, `isEmphasized` and a
  `tone`. Where you cannot render `Text`, the element takes one `.sd-type-<role>-<size>` class
  ([`shared-classes.md`](shared-classes.md)).
- **Never set type per property.** Not `font-size: var(--sd-type-body-medium-font-size)` beside your
  own `font-weight`: a role is a composite of size, weight, line height and tracking tuned together
  per brand, and pulling one property out breaks the set. Never a literal font size or weight.
- **Pick the role by what the text does, not how it should look.** `title` names a view or a
  surface; `subtitle` heads a compact unit; `body` is reading content or a value; `label` names a
  control, a field or a value; `caption` annotates something else; `display` and `headline` are
  hero scale only; `code` is monospace. The size is `medium` unless a prop drives it or the text
  reads one rung below a partner seen with it.
- **Pick the ink by function.** Text inherits its surface's ink by default. A supporting line under
  a primary one is `muted`; a mark the product flags with no status attached (a sale price) is
  `emphasis`; a reason to act now (a deal ending) is `urgency`; an error or a warning takes that
  status's text role. Through `Text` that is `tone`; in your own CSS it is the matching
  `--sd-color-text-*` role. An `on-*` ink is read only on its own fill.

# Theming

The attributes that select how Sando units look at runtime: which brand, light or dark, more
contrast, frosted overlays, an inverse ground, a usage context. Each is a `data-*` attribute you set
yourself; the brand sheets react to it. Look one up here when you wire a theme switch, a dark mode
toggle or a kiosk build.

Hand-maintained. Every selector and value below was read off the brand sheets and `tokens.css` of
the release this guide ships with; it states no token value.

## The attributes at a glance

| Attribute | Where | Values | When absent |
|---|---|---|---|
| `data-brand` | `<html>` | the name of an installed brand sheet | the default brand sheet applies |
| `data-theme` | `<html>` | `light`, `dark` | follows the OS colour scheme |
| `data-contrast` | `<html>` | `more` | follows the OS contrast preference, where the brand sheet supports it |
| `data-surface` | `<html>` | `translucent` | overlays are opaque |
| `data-context` | `<html>` | a usage context the brand sheet declares | no context: the brand's own sizes |
| `data-ground` | any element | `inverse` | the subtree follows the page |

Every brand sheet scopes its rules to the document root (`html:root[...]`), so the five root
attributes do nothing on a wrapper element. They belong on `<html>` because Dialog, Popover, Drawer,
Menu and the other overlays portal to `<body>`, and the root is the only ancestor they share with
the page.

## Brand: the default sheet and the others

Each brand is one stylesheet under `src/styles/themes/`, holding that brand's whole set of colour,
size, radius and type values. `tokens.css` holds none of them, so at least one brand sheet must be
loaded.

- **The default brand sheet** hangs on plain `:root`. It applies with no attribute, and also when
  `data-brand` names a brand you did not install. Its header comment says it is the default. The
  `styles` item installs it with every unit.
- **Every other brand sheet** is scoped to `data-brand="<name>"` and paints nothing without it. Its
  header comment names the exact value. Installing a `brand-<name>` item adds one.

```html
<html lang="en" data-brand="<name>">
```

The sheets are written so that import order never decides the winner: with both loaded, the named
brand wins over the default in any order. Switching brands at runtime is setting the attribute;
every brand sheet you might switch to has to be imported.

A brand sheet works only with the `tokens.css` of the same release. Upgrade them together, as
[getting-started.md](getting-started.md) § Upgrading describes.

## Dark mode: `data-theme`

Every brand carries its own light and dark values.

- No attribute: light, switching to dark when the OS prefers a dark colour scheme
  (`prefers-color-scheme: dark`).
- `data-theme="dark"`: dark, whatever the OS says.
- `data-theme="light"`: light, whatever the OS says.

There is no `auto` value. To return to following the OS, remove the attribute. Any value other than
`light` or `dark` matches neither the dark rules nor the OS rule, so it renders light and ignores the
OS.

```ts
// A three-way toggle
const root = document.documentElement
if (choice === 'system') root.removeAttribute('data-theme')
else root.setAttribute('data-theme', choice) // 'light' | 'dark'
```

Set it before first paint (an inline script in `<head>`, or server-rendered markup) if you store the
choice, or the page flashes the OS theme first.

## More contrast: `data-contrast`

`data-contrast="more"` switches to the brand's high-contrast values. With no attribute, the OS
preference (`prefers-contrast: more`) turns it on. It combines with `data-theme`, so a brand that
supports it has four colour states: light, dark, and each with more contrast.

- `more` is the only value that turns it on. Any other value turns it off and also stops the OS
  preference from turning it on, which makes `data-contrast="no-preference"` a way to opt out.
- Not every brand ships high-contrast values. A sheet that does contains `[data-contrast="more"]`
  rules; on a sheet without them the attribute does nothing.

## Frosted overlays: `data-surface`

`data-surface="translucent"` turns the overlay layer into frosted glass: Dialog, Drawer, Popover, and
with Popover every anchored overlay (Menu, Select, ComboBox, the date pickers). With no attribute,
overlays are opaque. Text on the translucent surface keeps its contrast; the opacity is derived for
that.

It is a whole-app choice. There is no per-overlay prop, so either every overlay is glass or none is.
Every brand sheet carries both treatments.

## Inverse ground: `data-ground`

`data-ground="inverse"` on any element switches that element's subtree to the opposite theme: dark
values on a light page, light values on a dark page, high contrast included where the brand has it.
`reset.css` re-inks the text inside it. This is the one attribute that is not for `<html>`.

You rarely set it by hand. `Band` with `tone="inverse"` sets it for a page section. An overlay opened
from inside the subtree portals out of it, so it shows the page's theme, not the inverse one.

## Usage context: `data-context`

`data-context` declares how a screen is used, and moves sizes (control heights, type, spacing, icons)
to suit that device. It is never inferred from screen size; your app sets it. It holds one value at
a time.

Every brand sheet declares these two:

| Value | For |
|---|---|
| `kiosk-standing` | a customer standing at a self-service kiosk, in its normal mode |
| `kiosk-accessible` | the same kiosk in its accessibility mode, with larger type and controls |

A brand sheet may declare more of its own; search the sheet for `data-context="` to see
which it has. A value the sheet does not declare changes nothing.

## Reacting to the theme in your own CSS

Read Sys tokens (`--sd-color-*`, `--sd-space-*` and the rest) and your CSS follows every attribute
above with no extra rule. Do not rebuild the cascade yourself with `[data-theme="dark"] .my-thing`
or a `prefers-color-scheme` query: it misses the OS-preference case, contrast and the inverse
ground, and breaks when a brand changes its values. The rules for your own CSS are
[styling-contract.md](styling-contract.md).

## One theme per product

Your product uses one brand: the default, or one `brand-<name>` item you install. Its screens are
designed against it, so set that brand's `data-brand` once and do not swap it for another. A
product that truly ships under several brands lists each in `design/product.json` `theme`, and
`sando verify` renders every screen in each ([design-language.md](design-language.md)
§ design/product.json).

## A new theme is made in Sando

You cannot build a brand sheet in your own repo. A sheet is generated from the brand's colour, type,
scale and interaction settings, and checked for contrast, rendering and Figma parity before it ships.
To get a new theme, or to change one, ask Sando for it; it arrives as a `brand-<name>` item you
install like any other. Do not override Sys tokens in your own CSS to fake one.

## Fonts

A brand names its font families but ships no `@font-face`. You host and load the faces yourself;
until you do, text falls back to the system font. Which faces each brand uses and how to load them:
[typefaces.md](typefaces.md).

## How to load

Pick one approach. Both self-host or pin versions; do **not** rely on a viewer having the font
installed locally (see the `local()` gotcha below). The examples load the **default brand**'s faces
(Pretendard, listed under Hangul in its table, is the whole stack of both text slots, Latin
included; IBM Plex Mono fills `mono`). For another brand, load
the families and weights its own table lists instead.

### A. npm packages (bundler apps, recommended)

```bash
npm install pretendard @fontsource/ibm-plex-mono
```

```ts
// import once at your app root, before Sando styles
import "pretendard/dist/web/static/pretendard.css";   // display and sans slots, Latin and Hangul, 300 to 700
import "@fontsource/ibm-plex-mono/400.css";           // mono slot: code · kbd
import "@fontsource/ibm-plex-mono/500.css";           // mono's emphasized twin
```

A brand whose table lists its own `sans` or `display` family adds one import per family; most open
faces are published as `@fontsource/<family>` or `@fontsource-variable/<family>`.

> Take the **variable** package only when its declared family name matches the stack. Some do
> (`@fontsource-variable/archivo` declares plain `"Archivo"`), some do not
> (`@fontsource-variable/inter` declares `"Inter Variable"`, which no Sando stack names). Check
> before swapping, or the face silently never applies.

### B. Drop-in `<style>` (no bundler)

Paste this into your document `<head>`, **before** `tokens.css`. It declares each face with
`url()` only (see below).

```html
<style>
  /* display and sans slots: Pretendard, Latin and Hangul */
  @font-face { font-family: "Pretendard"; font-weight: 300; font-display: swap;
    src: url("https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/pretendard@1.3.9/dist/web/static/woff2/Pretendard-Light.woff2") format("woff2"); }
  @font-face { font-family: "Pretendard"; font-weight: 400; font-display: swap;
    src: url("https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/pretendard@1.3.9/dist/web/static/woff2/Pretendard-Regular.woff2") format("woff2"); }
  @font-face { font-family: "Pretendard"; font-weight: 500; font-display: swap;
    src: url("https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/pretendard@1.3.9/dist/web/static/woff2/Pretendard-Medium.woff2") format("woff2"); }
  @font-face { font-family: "Pretendard"; font-weight: 600; font-display: swap;
    src: url("https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/pretendard@1.3.9/dist/web/static/woff2/Pretendard-SemiBold.woff2") format("woff2"); }
  @font-face { font-family: "Pretendard"; font-weight: 700; font-display: swap;
    src: url("https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/pretendard@1.3.9/dist/web/static/woff2/Pretendard-Bold.woff2") format("woff2"); }

  /* mono slot: IBM Plex Mono. 500 as well: `code`'s emphasized twins declare `medium` and this
     family is not variable, so it would otherwise be synthesised. */
  @font-face { font-family: "IBM Plex Mono"; font-weight: 400; font-display: swap;
    src: url("https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@fontsource/ibm-plex-mono@5.1.1/files/ibm-plex-mono-latin-400-normal.woff2") format("woff2"); }
  @font-face { font-family: "IBM Plex Mono"; font-weight: 500; font-display: swap;
    src: url("https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@fontsource/ibm-plex-mono@5.1.1/files/ibm-plex-mono-latin-500-normal.woff2") format("woff2"); }
</style>
```

For a brand with its own Latin face, add one `@font-face` per weight its table lists (or one with a
`font-weight` range for a variable file), named exactly as the table names the family.

## Why `url()` only, no `local()`

The declarations above intentionally omit `local()`. Upstream CDN CSS (Pretendard's, for one) lists
`local()` **first**, which lets a locally installed weight (often Regular only) hijack a heavier
slot: the browser binds a Regular face to `font-weight: 700`, renders headings thin, and never
downloads the real Bold. `url()` only bypasses this.

## No fonts loaded?

That is fine: every stack ends in a generic family and the components stay usable. `sans` and
`display` both end `system-ui, sans-serif` and `mono` ends `monospace`. What an unloaded face costs
depends on the brand: with two voices the headings lose their character and the body keeps its own;
with one face in both slots the whole type voice goes at once. Either way the size and weight
hierarchy survives, because tokens carry it rather than the font file.

If you render Korean and load nothing, the Hangul falls to the OS default, a different face on
every machine. That is the one fallback worth closing even in a prototype.
